answer.why: As an insider, 'Confirmed & Substantive' made me laugh straight away because it is exactly the appraisal and appointment language we all know, the moment you stop being acting and it is official. 'Minister Salary' is the line every outsider reaches for, the kopitiam punchline, and I would worry it is a cheap satire or a rant about pay, though I might still tap out of curiosity.
answer.expect_minister_salary: A blunt, slightly clickbaity game about the famous ministerial pay benchmark, probably leaning on the political controversy. I would expect a cynical or tongue-in-cheek take, an outsider's view of the service with a fixation on money and the top of the pyramid, and I would brace for wrong details about grades and processes. Easy to understand at a glance and it would get more taps from the general public.
answer.expect_confirmed_substantive: A dry, insider-flavoured career sim about the slow grind of promotion, acting appointments, appraisals and being made permanent. I would expect it to be accurate and wry about bureaucratic life, with jokes only public servants get. It is less obvious to outsiders and sounds a bit like a legal or HR term, but to me it promises authenticity and a quiet sense of humour.

best_moment.what: Conceding publicly that the Forum letter was correct. It is exactly the kind of small, unglamorous call that real officers remember, and it felt true to the service.

worst_moment.what: Being introduced as a GRC candidate and finding the single seat locked because REP was 58, below 60. The gate was invisible until it shut, so it felt like a stat check rather than a decision.

answer.held_back_by: REP, the stat I never saw coming. I kept building substance and integrity, but the game wanted visibility and a public profile at the end. Honest, solid, dependable officers do not necessarily win wards, and it never told me that early enough to act on it.
answer.ending_fair_why: Losing at 48.2 percent was believable, and the line that it was never about me rang true. But I did the honest thing at every turn, and the game never showed that REP would decide the end. It felt like a hidden requirement rather than a consequence of my choices.
answer.chase_next: I would chase the ministerial appointment. This time I would build REP early, perhaps by choosing to be seen more often, and see whether I can win a seat and the portfolio, since the salary benchmark is the thing the title promises.
answer.play_again_why: I want to know whether the folder ever pays off and whether a higher REP changes the ending. The run was short enough to try again on another commute.

tone_breaks.note: A GRC team contests a GRC, and a ward is a smaller division within it. The heading and the single seat versus GRC logic blur the electoral mechanics a little, so an insider would wince.

tone_breaks.line: RETIRED AS Permanent Secretary AT AGE 51
tone_breaks.note: The Perm Sec was labelled Staff Grade in my notes, and retiring at 51 after a lost election feels abrupt. A Perm Sec who runs and loses would not usually be cast off like this.

answer.title_fit_why: The game was about slow, quiet things: appraisal wording, the tea invitation, being nominated by someone you once helped. Those are what the career is about. The salary figure was a number at the end, not what drove my choices.
